title: El semáforo del argot
summary: Spain's slang traffic-light: green (guay, mola), yellow (tío, flipar, currar), red (joder, coño, hostia) — flagged honestly, recognition first

blocks.title: El semáforo del argot
blocks.body: Spain slangs and swears **far more freely** than English speakers expect — but not everything is safe everywhere. Think of it as a **traffic light**. 🟢 **Verde**: safe with anyone. 🟡 **Amarillo**: friends and peers, not strangers or *usted*. 🔴 **Rojo**: genuinely strong — real swearing. Today's rule for red: **recognize it before you reproduce it**.
blocks.callout: The goal isn't to swear. It's to *understand* Spain and control your own register.

blocks.title: Las tres luces
blocks.body: Learn where each word sits. The reds are common in casual Spain — you **will** hear them — but they stay off-limits in any formal, service or professional setting, and never with *usted*.

rows: tío/a, flipar, currar, pasta, movida, chungo

blocks.title: 🟡 Amarillo: entre colegas
blocks.body: These are the everyday slang of friends — warm, informal, but out of place with a stranger or your boss. **tío/tía** (mate/dude), **flipar** (to be amazed — *flipo contigo*), **currar** (to work; *el curro* = the job), **pasta** (money/dough), **movida** (a hassle/scene), **chungo** (dodgy/rough/tricky). Use them with the cast; drop them in a job interview.
blocks.callout: *Menuda movida* = what a mess. *Está la cosa chunga* = things are tricky.

blocks.title: 🔴 Rojo: reconócelo, no lo sueltes
blocks.body: Spain uses **joder** (damn / stronger), **coño** (a strong 'damn / hell') and **hostia / la hostia** (bloody hell) casually among friends — genuinely more than English does. But they are **real swearing**. The honest rule: **learn to recognize them** so you understand what's said, and hold off using them until you truly feel the register. **Never** with *usted*, never in a shop, an office, or with someone you've just met.
blocks.callout: *¡La hostia!* can also mean 'amazing' (*es la hostia* = it's brilliant) — same word, opposite feel. Context is everything.

blocks.prompt: Estás en una entrevista de trabajo. ¿Qué frase NO deberías usar?
blocks.explain: **Joder** is red-tier swearing and **flipar** is yellow slang — both are wrong in an interview. Keep it neutral: *me interesa mucho el proyecto*.

blocks.prompt: Type the green-tier way to say 'it's really cool' (use *mola* + an intensifier).
blocks.explain: *Mola mucho* — safe with anyone, warm and very Spain. *Mola un montón* works too.

blocks.scene: Rafa tells you about a rough day at the bookshop — spot the register

lines.speaker: Rafa
lines.target: Tío, menudo día de curro llevo.
lines.en: Mate, what a workday I'm having.

lines.speaker: Rafa
lines.target: Buah, el ordenador se ha roto y he perdido un pedido gordo. Joder.
lines.en: Ugh, the computer broke and I lost a big order. Damn.
lines.spotlight: *Joder* is red-tier — Rafa uses it among friends. You recognize it; you don't have to copy it.

lines.speaker: You
lines.target: Jolín, qué chungo. ¿Y la pasta del pedido?
lines.en: Darn, that's rough. And the money from the order?

lines.speaker: Rafa
lines.target: Pues la recupero, pero flipo con la mala suerte.
lines.en: I'll get it back, but I can't believe my bad luck.

lines.speaker: Lucía
lines.target: Venga, hombre, invito yo a la caña. Que no ha sido para tanto.
lines.en: Come on, my treat on the beer. It wasn't that big a deal.

lines.speaker: Rafa
lines.target: Eres la leche, Lucía. Gracias, tía.

questions.q: ¿Por qué está Rafa de mal humor?
options: Ha perdido un pedido en el curro
roja, fuerte — mejor reconocer que repetir

blocks.prompt: Haz tu propio semáforo. Escribe una palabra 🟢 verde, una 🟡 amarilla y una 🔴 roja que hayas oído en España, y anota con quién la usarías (o no). Sé honesto/a con el registro.
